morning.title: China’s J-35 3D Printing Push Offers AMCA a Lesson
morning.text:
China is leveraging Additive Manufacturing (AM) technologies for their fighter development and this can teach us some valuable lessons for the Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA) programme, as we look to narrow down our Development-cum-Production Partner. Our chosen industry partner must invest in advanced manufacturing technologies from the get-go. This will reduce the number of parts needed whilst making the manufacturing process simpler.
According to a report published by China’s Global Times on November 14, the Shenyang Aircraft Design and Research Institute, which designs the J-35 series of fighters, have made great strides in using AM for aircraft structures. They have successfully manufactured an integral load-carrying component that is over five metres long using 3D printing, the institute announced in a statement by Aviation Industry Corporation of China (AVIC).
This component sits in the aircraft’s centre fuselage and is used to carry and transfer structural loads. This is an important milestone because traditionally, this kind of part would have many different sections that need to be machined and then joined together.
A multi-functional annular heat exchanger has been developed by the Chinese lab. This fits within the aircraft’s intakes and combines heat transfer, air extraction, load carrying and servicing. The heat exchanger has channels within it that have been 3D printed to increase heat transfer surface area and reduce weight.
AVIC also revealed that they have developed six AM technologies, thirteen different metal materials and nineteen different categories of aircraft structure components using AM. This has taken place over a period of two decades+ so China will have invested substantially into this programme.
This is particularly important for India, as we have three private sector groups shortlisted by the Aeronautical Development Agency (ADA). These groups are Tata Advanced Systems, Larsen & Toubro led consortium (Bharat Electronics & Dynamatic Technologies) and Bharat Forge led consortium (BEML & Data Patterns).
The Request for Proposal was released in May 2026 with proposals due by October 30. Technical proposals were opened the next day. The chosen partner will work alongside the ADA to develop five flying prototypes and one structural test aircraft. The government will fund this prototyping stage with a budget of around ₹15,000 crore. The partner will be chosen around early 2027.
The winning DCPP should utilise AM technologies throughout their AMCA industrial strategy.
A modern stealth fighter aircraft will contain thousands of components. These can include structural brackets, ducting, cooling, electronics housings, mounting brackets and complex internal components. Many of these components will have complex shapes that can be difficult or costly to manufacture.
Metal AM can be used to create very complex shapes, with internal cooling channels and consolidate parts that would generally require multiple parts. This will reduce the number of joints, bolts and can improve the weight efficiency. Engineers can also iterate and prototype quicker without having to create expensive tooling.
This can be leveraged for the AMCA too. Complex aerospace components are often manufactured using many different machining processes. A well qualified AM process can reduce some of these processes, remove the need for specialist tooling and reduce the lead time of manufacture.
We have a good base to build upon. The DRDO’s Defence Metallurgical Research Laboratory are working on metal AM. The DRDO Industry Academia Centre of Excellence at IIT Hyderabad has demonstrated a large scale AM system in January 2025. The machine uses powder based Directed Energy Deposition and has a build size of 1mx1mx3m. They have successfully printed a metal component of around 1m.
India has also demonstrated metal 3D printing on aircraft engines. HAL and Wipro 3D have created a Nozzle Guide Vane for a helicopter engine using high temperature resistant A286 steel. This component has been certified as airworthy.
There will be lots of investment required to go from single certified components to large primary components. The AMCA DCPP should invest in bespoke AM facilities. This will include metal 3D printing machines, advanced material laboratories, automated inspection, heat treatment facilities and precise post processing.
Investment will also need to be made into qualifying the components. Just because you can 3D print a component doesn’t mean it is suitable for flight. The material properties must be consistent, porosity, stress, fatigue, dimensional accuracy and consistency must be proven.
The aim shouldn’t be to fully 3D print the fighter. The ADA and partner should identify what components can be manufactured using AM to give weight, strength, faster manufacturing or lower costs.
EDITED BY RAUNAK KUNDE

morning.title: MoD to Select Partner for DRDO’s Rudram-III Anti-Radiation Missile
morning.text:
The Ministry of Defence (MoD) is expected to select a private sector company as a production partner for the Rudram-III that has been India’s Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO). IDRW has been told by its sources that until now only Bharat Dynamics Limited (BDL) has been its primary production partner for the missile system, and MoD is keen to have another set of production lines that can cater to both the IAF’s requirements and that of the export.
Rudram-III has completed captive flight trials from the Su-30MKI, and further software and hardware optimisation is ongoing so that it will be India’s go-to weapon for SEAD and DEAD missions, and further improvements are being made so that it can handle a larger variety of targets in the future.
With development trials to be started soon, MoD is keen that a private sector company be roped in to the programme so that it can get its hand on prototype working, and by the time the missile is ready for production, the private sector company will be in a position to handle ramping up the production and also have a trained crew to handle the production of the missile itself.
IDRW has been told that many companies from the private sector have shown interest in setting up production lines for many missiles that are now open for production for private sector companies, and Rudram-III is one of the weapon systems that will be on offer for complete ToT so that the missile system can be manufactured by a private sector company.
Rudram-I and Rudram-II have already been given to private sector companies like Adani Defence for local manufacturing of the weapons systems, and Rudram-III is already generating interest from many private sector companies, and Adani Defence might not be the default choice as its production partner, as per sources close to IDRW.
Rudram-III has been designed to penetrate even highly defended key installations, and each Su-30MKI will be able to carry four Rudram-III externally, and many other jets like Mirage-2000 and Rafale, including Tejas MkII, will also feature them when they are cleared for production, so the expected requirements for the IAF might be on the higher side, and demand for the missile system will only grow as the missile is cleared for operations from other jets in multiple phases.
IDRW has estimated that the IAF might have combined long-term requirements for at least 1500 units of the missile for the entire fighter fleet, from which it wants to operate the missile, and close to 500 units might be procured from the first batch itself since the IAF has a bigger Su-30MKI fleet, and each aircraft can carry four units of this missile; thus, the majority of the first batch order will be reserved for the Su-30MKI batch.
RAUNAK KUNDE

morning.title: Anti-India content is now an online biz model
morning.text: Tanvi Jhansi Rajgarhia, a content creator from Mumbai who mixes her music with liberal politics as well as protein targets on social media posts, flew to New York three years ago with an artist visa in her hand and Broadway dreams in her eyes. But she faced something unexpected-vicious online hate. As she made comedic content on Indian American supporters of MAGA over a cup of chai and made political jokes about Donald Trump, his Qatari jet and Indian WhatsApp uncles flabbergasted by tariffs, she faced a barrage of hate comments and even threats. In October 2025, fearing for her safety, she took a flight back to Mumbai."What affected me most was the hate in comments and direct messages that included curses, slurs and threats," recalls Rajgarhia, 31. "Once I was even threatened in person by someone who recognised my content."136066001Back in the US, when she scrolled the replies to her Insta posts, she came across a word-pajeet. It looked familiar and sounded innocent, but it was not. A fabricated word, it is a racist slur used online at Indians. The Punjabi-sounding word, which first appeared on an anonymous messaging board of 4chan in 2015, insulting Indians over open defecation, now crops up across posts, videos and memes in mainstream online platforms.While Rajgarhia was at the receiving end of ugly racism, hate is not confined to DMs. Social media posts targeting Indians go viral, garnering millions of views. The massive Indian presence on Meta platforms and X adds fuel to the fire. What lies behind anti-India inflammatory content? Is it racism, engagement farming, or both?136065967Target IndiaOn September 13, Bo French, an anti-immigration Republican politician from Texas, posted on X a photograph of students, who looked like South Asians, celebrating a football victory by the University of Texas. He wrote: "I heard UT graduation this year looked like this. I didn't believe it. The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined." While many in the Republican Party have distanced themselves from his xenophobic post, it has got about 55 million views.In such inflammatory posts, Indians are targeted mainly over immigration, poverty and hygiene.The Center for the Study of Organized Hate (CSOH), a think tank based in Washington, DC, studied 680 high-engagement anti-India racist posts on X between July 1 and September 7, 2025. They got over 281 million views in total. The posts about a Florida truck crash involving a Sikh driver in August 2025 alone had about 95 million views."There is a noticeable increase in anti-Indian rhetoric online," says Sumitra Badrinathan, assistant professor of political science at the School of International Service, American University. The rise in online outrage parallels the immigration crackdown by Trump. Joyojeet Pal, professor of information at the University of Michigan, says there has been a dramatic increase in a new kind of anti-immigrant sentiment in US, especially since the second Trump administration.136066004Badrinathan sees three broad narratives recurring in the hate content: economic resentment against Indian immigrants "taking" American jobs, racialised stereotypes around hygiene, food and poverty with selective or misleading images, and claims of cultural or religious incompatibility between Indians and Western societies.Battle For ViewsFor content creators, engagement means earnings. Says Rajgarhia: "Everyone is incentivised by money or fame when they are posting anti-India content. And it works because Indians jump to their own defence." For content creators seeking brand deals, numbers are the dealmaker. "Engagement is the currency. Higher engagement translates into higher earnings. If I have a lot of engagement, my manager can negotiate on my behalf and get a bigger deal for me," she adds.Tanmoy Chakraborty, an IIT-Delhi professor who researches hate-speech detection, says hateful online users rely on tightly connected, like-minded groups or echo chambers to quickly boost and spread their posts. The online-outrage business goes beyond direct earnings from posts to paid services. Chakraborty says there are also "collusive users" who spread misinformation and hate speech at the behest of agencies for money.Why does rage bait work at scale on Indians? Because of their sheer numbers. India and China are the most populous countries-whereas Facebook, Instagram and X are officially blocked in mainland China, Indians are thronging them, falling for clickbait comments, arguing, dissing and, in the process, making even anti-India content go viral.According to online research platform DataReportal, Facebook had 403 million users and Instagram had over 480 million users in India in 2025. X has about 23 million active users from India.Rajiv Ratn Shah, associate professor in the Department of Intelligent Systems at IIT-Kanpur, says, "There is a huge presence of Indians on social media platforms. And they engage with content with which they have cultural proximity and familiarity."136066026Even negative reaction is engagement. Prateek Waghre, a Bengaluru-based technology-policy researcher, calls this "algorithmic reward". He says platforms treat engagement-"whether it's positive or negative, in agreement or in disagreement"-as a sign of interest. "When more people engage with a content, it's put on more people's feeds, and then even more people engage with it."136066007Now AI has made the field messier because of the ease with which one can create believable, realistic-looking fake content. "The believability of posts has increased significantly because of AI," says Chakraborty.An AI-generated video of a man rolling rotis on his bare stomach spread widely enough to be logged in the AI Incidents Monitor of the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development.Pamposh Raina, head of the Deepfakes Analysis Unit at Trusted Information Alliance, a Delhi-based information integrity coalition, says that her team focuses on verifying and analysing harmful and misleading AI-generated content.They examined deceptive food-hygiene videos that had real footage stitched with synthetic audio. Some clips were only around 10 seconds long and had background noise or music added, which complicates AI detection.A major news event offers a readymade opportunity for bad actors to get views, she says. "They create counter narratives to confuse and mislead people." Some of it, she adds, is "a function of people making money out of it".136065973Rules On PaperThere is a caveat, say social media companies in their defence: it is not easy to monetise hate content. At least on paper. In response to ET's queries, a YouTube spokesperson says the platform's hate speech policy prohibits content promoting violence or hatred against people on grounds like ethnicity, nationality, race and religion. Earning advertising revenue requires a membership of the YouTube Partner Programme and compliance with its advertiser-friendly guidelines, the spokesperson adds.In its response, Meta points to Instagram's feed recommendations, which say posts must meet its quality and integrity rules. Content that exploits controversial political or social issues for commercial purposes is also restricted from monetisation.The test of the first point, says Pal, lies in platform data that shows whether people have encountered hate posts through recommendations.(X has not responded to ET's queries at the time of going to press.)While social media platforms can theoretically restrict the reach of violative content, like hate posts on India, its virality means enforcement remains poor, says Waghre. He adds that there are multiple reasons for this: "One, they are not detected due to scale or because posters use coded language that platforms don't understand. Two, they are detected but platforms believe they don't violate their community guidelines which could just be a wrong call, or a result of them not having the necessary context or understanding."The social media companies' argument falls apart on further scrutiny. The Global Disinformation Index, a UK-based nonprofit, found that most of the hateful content it tracked on YouTube was permitted and monetised on the platform. It estimates that 100 such English-language channels are on track to earn $13.3 million in ad revenue in 2026, with anti-immigrant hate earning the most.Monetisation on YouTube and Insta happens mostly through brand partnerships, sponsored content, subscriptions and affiliate links, while X reportedly pays according to the number of verified impressions for a post.Real-World ImpactOnline hate has real-world impact, like it did for Rajgarhia. In Carnegie's Indian American Attitudes Survey of 2026, conducted across 1,000 Indian American adults, 48% said they had encountered racist social media posts targeting Indians very or somewhat often. Half the respondents felt angry when they saw such posts, 48% felt anxious and 31% felt fearful. Since 2025, when Trump came to power for his second term, one-third of them avoided political discussions on social media, concerned about discrimination or racism directed towards Indians or Indian Americans.The Indian American Attitudes Survey also recorded direct experiences of anti-Indian hate. About a quarter of Indian Americans said they were called a racial or ethnic slur since the start of 2025, while 9% reported physical threats and 4% reported physical assault.In October, it was on the brink of becoming a mass tragedy. Alexandros Paporakis, a teenager from Illinois, US, who calls himself a white supremacist, told his coworker at Taco Bell that he wanted to kill Indians and that he tried to attack a Hindu temple on the first day of Navratri, but his gun got jammed. He was indicted earlier this week by a jury.The consumption of inflammatory content hurts not just the target audience; it can also deleteriously reinforce biases and prejudices. Rituparna Patgiri, assistant professor of sociology at IIT-Guwahati, says, "If you are repeatedly consuming a particular content, your views get influenced."Identifying and removing such content is not easy or straightforward. Badrinathan says platforms must enforce existing rules, make their recommendation systems more transparent and give researchers better data access to check compliance.Until then, the hate mills will keep turning.

morning.title: Review: Godzilla Minus Zero joins the list of truly stellar sequels
morning.text:
It's a rare thing for a film sequel to match or even surpass its predecessor; The Godfather Part II and Terminator 2: Judgement Day are the best known examples on a pretty short list. Go ahead and add Godzilla Minus Zero to that list. Director Takashi Yamazaki's sequel to his critically acclaimed Godzilla Minus One (2023) is everything one could want in a Godzilla movie: human pathos, great special effects, and, ultimately, two giant kaiju duking it out over who gets to destroy Japan (and eventually the world) the most.

(Spoilers for the first film below. Spoilers for Minus Zero but no major reveals until after the gallery. We'll give you a heads-up when we get there.)

As I wrote previously, Yamazaki wanted to return to Godzilla’s filmic roots with Minus One, setting the events in postwar Japan and tapping into the monster’s symbolic representation of the Japanese perspective on the 1940s nuclear holocaust—while also incorporating all-too-human themes of guilt and redemption. morning.title: Industry body raises alarm: 689 tenders for Chinese drones & parts floated since 2021, 84% by Army
morning.text:
New Delhi: As many as 689 tenders floated on the Government e-Marketplace (GeM) by the military, security forces and others over nearly six years were found to specify Chinese drones and drone components, 355 of them this year alone, the Drone Federation India (DFI) has told defence officials.
The Army alone accounted for 580 (84 percent) of the tenders over the full period and 328 (92 percent) of those put up in 2026.
The Border Security Force (BSF) follows with 12 tenders (1.7 percent) over the full period. The Armed Forces Tribunal, the Controller General of Defence Accounts and the Centre for Development of Advanced Computing (C-DAC) have issued seven each (1 percent each).
The Jammu and Kashmir Police, the Directorate of Public Relations and the Directorate General of Defence Estates have five each (0.7 percent each). The remaining 61 tenders (8.9 percent) come from 44 other organisations.
Notably, GeM tenders specifying Chinese drones or drone parts nearly doubled from 190 in 2025 to 355 in 2026 up to 19 November, according to the DFI’s findings.
The DFI’s representation, dated 20 November, to the officials is based on its findings on tenders published between 10 March 2021 and 19 November 2026. The DFI says it had received reports of Army units procuring Chinese drone components, as well as knocked-down kits made up of Chinese components.
The DFI then studied publicly available bid documents on GeM and found that bids for Army procurement specify products of Chinese-linked brands, including EMAX, RunCam, SpeedyBee, RadioMaster, T-Motor, GEPRC and HGLRC. The items include motors, flight controllers, electronic speed controller (ESC) stacks, receivers, cameras and video transmission equipment, it adds.
“These are not peripheral accessories. They govern a drone’s flight, control and data transmission,” the DFI has cautioned.
The DFI is a non-government, not-for-profit industry body representing the domestic drone and counter-drone systems industry.
ThePrint reached out to the Army by email for comment. This report will be updated as and when a response is received.
“Most of the Army’s drone-related tenders from the past year or two are for drone parts, since it has recently begun assembling its own drones,” an industry source told ThePrint.
While acknowledging the Army’s role in enabling the government’s push to indigenise drones and drone components, including through initiatives such as the AASHVAST laboratory, the DFI found that 104 of the 328 flagged Army tenders from this year were raised after the laboratory was inaugurated 14 August.
An Army cybersecurity and firmware validation facility, the AASHVAST laboratory screens drones for Chinese-origin components, concealed code and remote-access mechanisms before being cleared for use.
According to the DFI’s findings, GeM tenders specifying Chinese drones or drone parts were few in the early years: six in 2021 (from 10 March), 36 in 2022, 60 in 2023 and 42 in 2024.
The sharp rise came after that. They grew 352 percent to 190 in 2025 and a further 87 percent to 355 in 2026, up to 19 November. The Army’s tenders followed the same pattern, rising from two in 2021 to 31 in 2024, then growing 419 percent to 161 in 2025 and 104 percent to 328 in 2026.
The DFI’s submission, which also seeks a meeting with officials, says the use of Chinese drones or components raises “serious security and industry concerns”.
When a bid specifically names such components, it argues, these risks enter at the tender stage itself, and it lists three risks.
First, components that units procure for their own internal use may escape further security screening, leaving units exposed to cyber vulnerabilities in flight control, communication and data. Second, with China’s export licensing of drone motors, ESCs, autopilots and radios in force from 18 November, supplies could be disrupted when they are most needed.
Third, if the user does not buy Indian components itself, the domestic component industry will not grow, and Indian manufacturers’ investments in indigenous design and secure supply chains will be undermined.
Noting that the domestic drone components ecosystem is still in its early phase, the DFI said, “It can mature only with assured demand from Indian users, and the armed forces are its most important user.”
The DFI has suggested that the authorities issue an advisory to all military formations, units and establishments to exclude Chinese components from drones and drone parts procured for internal use, including through GeM.
It has also called for reasonable preference to be given to Indian components, particularly critical parts such as flight controllers, receivers and data links, video transmitters, global navigation satellite system modules, cameras, motors, ESCs, and batteries.
Another suggestion is that a country-of-origin declaration, along with traceability at the component level, be made mandatory in all future bids related to drones, so that security is built into the specification and not left to checks after procurement.
Offering to help identify Indian alternatives at short notice, the DFI suggested that its Bharat Drone Stack Platform could be used to find Indian sources for these components. Launched in August 2025, the Bharat Drone Stack initiative lists more than 200 Indian component makers and aims to bridge the gap between them and drone integrators.
According to the DFI, the initiative targets 90 percent indigenisation in drone components by 2030, a Rs 15,000-crore domestic component market, a 75 percent cut in imports, as well as generating more than 5,000 new jobs and roping in over 500 Indian suppliers.
(Edited by Tony Rai)

morning.title: Building armed unmanned boats for the Navy: How Sagar Defence is chasing a $2 billion-plus valuation
morning.text:
New Delhi: Sagar Defence Engineering, which began life in 2015 in what was reportedly a cramped Mumbai office of barely 150 square feet and is today delivering armed unmanned boats to the Indian Navy, filed updated papers with the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) Thursday for a Rs 3,412-crore initial public offering (IPO).
The issue is made up of fresh shares worth Rs 1,200 crore and an offer for sale of Rs 2,212 crore, according to the company’s updated draft red herring prospectus. Before filing the updated papers, the company raised Rs 300 crore through a pre-IPO placement priced at Rs 97.27 a share, reducing the size of the fresh issue accordingly.
If the IPO is priced at the Rs 97.27 a share paid in the pre-IPO placement, Sagar Defence would be valued at about Rs 21,500 crore after the issue, according to ThePrint’s calculations based on its updated draft red herring prospectus.
The company’s registered office is in Mumbai, while its corporate office and both manufacturing facilities are in Chakan, Pune. It cites a CAREEdge report in the prospectus to describe itself as “the only company in India specialising in unmanned, integrated and multi-domain systems across the maritime surface, maritime sub-surface, aerial and land domains”.
Nikunj Parashar, the company’s founder, chairman and managing director, is a former merchant navy officer. His co-founders are Mridul Babbar, Lakshay Dang, Saurabh Patil and Ankit Kumar.
Addressing the Indian Navy’s ‘Swavlamban’ seminar last month, Parashar reportedly spoke of the setbacks he faced while building the company, including two heart attacks and a paralytic stroke.
At the core of Sagar Defence Engineering’s offering is ‘GENISYS’, its in-house autonomy and command-and-control system, which it markets as a combined hardware and software package that can turn existing vehicles into autonomous ones.
The company’s flagship offering is the ‘Matangi’ unmanned surface vessel, which in November 2024 reportedly made an uncrewed coast-to-coast passage of about 1,600 km from Mumbai in Maharashtra, on the west coast, to Thoothukudi in Tamil Nadu, on the south-eastern coast.
The Navy is reported to be taking delivery of 12 of the company’s armed unmanned surface vessels, ‘Matangi’ among them, under a contract awarded within the Innovations for Defence Excellence (iDEX) framework, with the boats said to carry 12.7 mm stabilised remote-controlled guns.
Sagar Defence also builds drones and has reportedly partnered with Israel Aerospace Industries on the ‘Point Blank’ loitering munition.
The company’s financials point to rapid growth. Revenue from operations climbed from Rs 39.50 crore in 2023-24 to Rs 254.59 crore in 2025-26, and the first six months of the current financial year, to 30 September, alone brought in Rs 222.24 crore. A loss of Rs 6.26 crore in 2023-24 turned into a profit of Rs 87.90 crore in 2025-26, and the company earned Rs 101.61 crore in profit in the first half of 2026-27.
The prospectus is also clear about the risks. “We derive almost all of our revenue from our top customer, i.e., the Government of India,” it states. The company also cautions that the drivers of its recent growth “may not be sustainable at historical rates”.
Most of the fresh capital, Rs 724.78 crore, is meant for a manufacturing and technology campus at Juvvaladinne Fishing Harbour in Andhra Pradesh’s Nellore district, pitched by the company as the country’s first autonomous maritime shipyard. Construction is yet to start, and the company concedes it has never run a coastal facility before. A further Rs 170 crore will go to research and development.
(Edited by Viny Mishra)

morning.title: India’s artillery push: 335 Vajras, proposals worth Rs 2.12 lakh crore including VVIP choppers cleared
morning.text:
New Delhi: The Defence Ministry Monday cleared proposals worth Rs 2.12 lakh-crore for military procurements, including a major push for artillery guns with plans to procure 335 more 155 mm/52 calibre K9 VAJRA-T self-propelled tracked guns.
The Defence Acquisition Council (DAC), chaired by Defence Minister Rajnath Singh, accorded Acceptance of Necessity (AoN)—in-principle administrative approval—to various capital acquisition proposals of the defence forces.
For the Indian Army, approval was accorded for the procurement of High Mobility Vehicles (HMV), Self-Propelled Tracked Gun System, Gun Shot Response System (GSRS), Light Multi Role Helicopters (LMRH), Very Short-Range Air Defence System (VSHORADS), Platform-Based Counter Unmanned Aerial System (C-UAS), Unmanned Aerial System Brick Long Range, Surveillance UAV, Integrated Surveillance and Strike System and Long Range Kamikaze Drone System, a statement by the Defence Ministry said.
Sources in the defence establishment said the Self-Propelled Tracked Gun System was the Vajra, 100 of which have been delivered and another 100 of which has been ordered for.
With the additional 335 now cleared for contract negotiations, Vajra will emerge as the mainstay of the Artillery regiments in times to come.
The number of 500 Vajras is well beyond the original Field Artillery Rationalisation Plan targets which was just 100.
In 2017, L&T won the Rs 4,500-crore contract to supply 100 K9 Vajras under ‘Make in India’ initiative for which it signed a transfer of technology contract with Hanwha Corporation.
According to L&T, the K9 Vajras were delivered with more than 80 percent indigenous work packages and above 50 percent indigenisation (by value) at the programme level.
When the Army did the trials for Vajras before selection, the trials were conducted in deserts and not in high-altitude areas where the howitzer’s systems work differently in rarefied atmosphere and extreme cold.
But with the tensions breaking out with China at the Line of Actual Control (LAC), the Army decided to deploy three of these tracked howitzers in Eastern Ladakh as a trial measure in 2020.
The three guns were fitted with winterisation kits that enabled them to work in sub-zero temperatures even though they were designed to operate in deserts. As reported by ThePrint, the gun system proved its mettle following which the Army deployed a full regiment (20 guns make one regiment) of these howitzers in Eastern Ladakh to add to its firepower.
The Self-Propelled Tracked Gun System will provide matching mobility and firepower to mechanised formations, the defence ministry statement added.
“The HMVs will enhance operational capabilities, logistic support and mobility in challenging terrains…The GSRS will serve as a force multiplier providing real-time situational awareness of the forces. The LMRH will be used by both the Indian Army and the Indian Air Force for Reconnaissance and Surveillance, Combat, Search and Rescue of troops, Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief etc.
“The VSHORADS will engage new generation small size aerial threats, while C-UAS will enhance survivability of Tanks in the modern battlefield. The Surveillance and Drone Systems will enhance the surveillance and targeting capabilities of the Indian Army,” the statement read.
For the Indian Navy, approval was given for the procurement of Active Offboard Decoy System (AODS) and other major Naval platforms.
The AODS will enhance the credibility of anti-missiles defence, especially against modern anti-ship missiles of adversaries. The indigenously designed and constructed major Naval platforms will possess modern-day warfare capabilities and enhance the combat capability of the Navy, the Defence ministry said.
VVIP choppers
For the Indian Air Force, approval was accorded for the procurement of helicopters, air defence systems, weapons and Mobile X-Band Doppler Weather Radar System to enhance air defence and war fighting capabilities.
The procurement of Special Utility Helicopters will help the IAF meet important air transport requirements, the defence ministry said.
Sources explained that this involves procurement of 24 choppers at an estimated cost of Rs 10,000 crore for transport of VVIPs, including the President, Vice-President and Prime Minister.
They will replace the current Russian Mi17- V5 helicopters in use.
The main competition will be between European Airbus and American Lockheed Martin.
(Edited by Ajeet Tiwari)
